canonical_statement: The document aims to provide practical clinical guidance for use of unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin, and fondaparinux in adults treated for venous thromboembolism.
The authors developed pivotal practical management questions for UFH, LMWH, and fondaparinux by author consensus.

The literature review searched PubMed and Medline and used the authors’ personal libraries, emphasizing high-quality cohort studies and randomized controlled trials from the prior 10 years when available.
For each practical question, the authors summarized and interpreted pertinent literature and existing guidelines, then provided a guidance recommendation.
The document explicitly uses consensus expert opinion where existing guidelines are lacking.
Before initiating UFH for acute VTE, obtain total body weight, CBC, PT, and aPTT.
For UFH treatment of acute VTE, efficacy is related to dose regardless of route, and the initial dose is considered more important than the aPTT for predicting efficacy.
The authors suggest the UFH initial dosing options in Table 2 while acknowledging that the listed regimens were not compared head-to-head.
Health systems are encouraged to audit UFH dose requirements against the responsiveness of their local aPTT reagent and coagulation instrument.
When a weight-based UFH strategy is used, total body weight is suggested for dose calculation.
For obese or morbidly obese patients receiving UFH, either total body weight or adjusted body weight may be used for dosing.
Evidence supporting total-body-weight UFH dosing in morbid obesity did not include patients weighing more than 270 kg.
Empiric UFH dose caps may increase the risk of initial under-anticoagulation in obese and morbidly obese patients and should allow individualized initial dosing when used.
Either aPTT or heparin anti-Xa monitoring may be used for UFH.
Heparin anti-Xa monitoring is suggested for UFH patients with heparin resistance, prolonged baseline aPTT, or altered heparin responsiveness.
For UFH monitoring, check aPTT or anti-Xa every 6 hours until two consecutive therapeutic results are obtained, then extend monitoring to once daily.
Continuous-infusion UFH should be monitored with aPTT or anti-Xa despite a weak evidence base, while monitoring is optional for subcutaneous weight-based UFH therapy.
The optimal UFH therapeutic range is uncertain, and ensuring an appropriate initial heparin dose is considered more important than the exact therapeutic range.
A one-time heparin-concentration-derived aPTT therapeutic range is recommended, with range re-evaluation after reagent or instrument changes.
When UFH is monitored with anti-Xa, the suggested therapeutic target is 0.3 to 0.7 units/mL.
When UFH resistance is suspected, obtain paired aPTT and heparin anti-Xa levels.
If aPTT is subtherapeutic but anti-Xa is therapeutic during suspected UFH resistance, no heparin dose adjustment is required and subsequent monitoring should use anti-Xa when feasible.
Persistently low aPTT and anti-Xa values despite serial UFH dose increases may indicate true heparin resistance.
UFH dosing adjustments should be guided by a dose-adjustment nomogram.
A weight-based UFH dose-adjustment algorithm may offer benefit over a fixed adjustment algorithm in obese patients.
More research is needed to define and assess the optimal UFH dose-adjustment nomogram.
UFH should overlap with warfarin for at least 5 days and until a single INR is 2.0 or greater.
For VTE treatment, rivaroxaban and apixaban do not require initial parenteral anticoagulation, whereas dabigatran and edoxaban require at least 5 days of parenteral anticoagulation before initiation.
Protamine sulfate is suggested to reverse UFH when reversal is indicated.
Health systems should develop and implement guidance for anticoagulant reversal and HIT evaluation and management.
Before initiating LMWH for acute VTE, obtain total body weight, baseline serum creatinine, CBC, PT, and aPTT.
For enoxaparin treatment of VTE, the authors suggest twice-daily dosing except in severe renal insufficiency.
Once-daily dalteparin may be used for treatment of both cancer-associated and non-cancer-associated VTE.
LMWH dosing should be based on total body weight in all patients, including underweight and obese patients.
For patients weighing less than 40 kg, UFH may be more appropriate than LMWH.
For obese patients treated with enoxaparin for VTE, 1 mg/kg twice daily is preferred over 1.5 mg/kg once daily.
Dose capping should be avoided for LMWH treatment dosing.
Routine peak anti-Xa monitoring is not recommended for LMWH in either obese or non-obese patients.
Renal function for LMWH dosing should be estimated with Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance.
In patients with creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min, UFH may be preferred over LMWH; if enoxaparin is used, the suggested dose is 1 mg/kg once daily.
If LMWH is continued beyond the usual 5 to 7 days, trough anti-Xa measurement may be considered in severe renal dysfunction.
LMWH should be avoided in patients with creatinine clearance below 20 mL/min and in patients receiving renal replacement therapy.
Patients receiving LMWH should be monitored for bleeding and for renal-function changes that may require dose adjustment.
CBC, platelet count, and serum creatinine should be assessed periodically during LMWH treatment.
Routine LMWH anti-Xa monitoring is discouraged.
In selected patients such as those with severe renal failure, trough anti-Xa levels may help evaluate LMWH accumulation and whether the dosing interval should be prolonged.
Peak anti-Xa levels should not be used to evaluate LMWH dosing regimens in clinical practice.
LMWH should overlap with warfarin for at least 5 days and until a single INR is 2.0 or greater.
For VTE treatment, rivaroxaban and apixaban do not require initial parenteral anticoagulation, whereas dabigatran and edoxaban require at least 5 days of parenteral anticoagulation before initiation.
When transitioning from LMWH to a target-specific oral anticoagulant, the first oral dose should be timed for when the next LMWH dose would have been due.
Patients with DVT and/or PE at low risk of complications may be treated as outpatients with LMWH when adequate home circumstances are present.
Protamine sulfate is suggested for reversal of LMWH when major bleeding occurs, with the last LMWH dose timing considered in the decision and dose.
A repeat protamine dose may be administered if bleeding continues or if aPTT remains prolonged 2 to 4 hours after the initial dose.
Patients who develop HIT in response to LMWH should be managed according to current HIT guidelines.
Before initiating fondaparinux for acute VTE, obtain total body weight, baseline serum creatinine, CBC, PT, and aPTT.
Fondaparinux treatment dosing is suggested by total body weight: 5 mg subcutaneously once daily below 50 kg, 7.5 mg once daily at 50 to 100 kg, and 10 mg once daily above 100 kg.
Fondaparinux should be dosed by total body weight, including in patients with BMI above 30 kg/m2.
Fondaparinux should be avoided when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min.
Patients with moderate renal insufficiency receiving longer courses of fondaparinux should be monitored closely for bleeding because of potential accumulation.
Most patients receiving fondaparinux do not require therapeutic drug monitoring.
If fondaparinux accumulation needs to be assessed, use an anti-Xa assay calibrated for fondaparinux rather than PT, aPTT, or ACT.
When trough fondaparinux levels are measured, use a chromogenic anti-Xa assay calibrated with fondaparinux rather than an assay standardized with LMWH or UFH.
Fondaparinux should overlap with warfarin for at least 5 days and until a single INR is 2.0 or greater.
For VTE treatment, rivaroxaban and apixaban do not require initial parenteral anticoagulation, whereas dabigatran and edoxaban require at least 5 days of parenteral anticoagulation before initiation.
When transitioning from fondaparinux to a target-specific oral anticoagulant, the first oral dose should be timed for when the next fondaparinux dose would have been due.
Patients with DVT and/or PE at low risk of complications may be treated as outpatients with fondaparinux when adequate home circumstances are present.
Fondaparinux may be used for VTE treatment in patients with a history of HIT.
For acute VTE with HIT developing after UFH or LMWH, fondaparinux may be considered as a treatment option and should be given at treatment doses if selected.
For life-threatening bleeding attributed to fondaparinux, rFVIIa is suggested, with potential benefit weighed against thrombotic risk.
The authors note that no high-quality data were available for any anticoagulant agent in the treatment of HIT.
Despite development of oral anticoagulants, parenteral heparins remain a component of VTE treatment and their appropriate use in special populations remains challenging.
